sections.body: Citizens usually have rights (vote, free speech, fair trial) and responsibilities (follow laws, pay taxes, serve on juries in some countries). These vary by country.
Elections work in different ways: first-past-the-post, proportional representation and others. Each has trade-offs.
Evaluating political claims: Is there evidence? Is the statistic in context? What do independent fact-checkers say? What would the other side say?
This lesson doesn't tell you what to think. Good citizens understand different views and decide with evidence.

quiz.q: A politician says 'Crime doubled!' What's the first thing to check?
options: The actual numbers, time period and source
hints: 'Cases doubled' from 1 to 2 is very different from 1,000 to 2,000.
quiz.explain: Check the real numbers, time period and source. 'Doubled' can mean very different things.

options: Seats are shared roughly in proportion to votes
The candidate with most votes in each area wins
hints: If a party gets 30% of votes…
In first-past-the-post, the top candidate in each area wins. Proportional systems do something different with the total vote.
quiz.explain: In proportional representation, parties get seats roughly in proportion to their share of the vote.
